title: Praying while traveling
hook: travelers shorten four-unit prayers to two, and may combine some

segments.voice: Yesterday, the khutbah: two sermons on Friday, heard in full silence. Today we leave the mosque and hit the road.

A highway rest stop, the engine ticking as it cools. A family has been on the road since breakfast, and the noon prayer has come in. The kids stretch their legs by a picnic table. Their father spreads a thin mat on the grass beside the car, faces the direction his phone gives him, prays, and is done sooner than at home. Shorter than usual, by design. Islam has a rule for the road, and it starts with a verse and a question someone once put to Umar.
screen: `A REST STOP, ENGINE COOLING.` → `A MAT ON THE GRASS.` → `SHORTER, BY DESIGN.`

segments.voice: Qasr means shortening. On a journey, the four-unit prayers, noon, afternoon and night, are prayed as two. Dawn and sunset stay as they are. First, the verse. Pickthall's translation of surah four says that when ye go forth in the land, "it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship," then adds a condition: if you fear an attack. Second, the question. A man named Ya'la asked Umar ibn al-Khattab: people are safe now, so why do we still shorten? Umar said he had wondered the same, and had asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who answered: it is a charity God has given you, so accept His charity. That's in Sahih Muslim. Four days ago, two units of duha were a charity paid for your joints. Here it runs the other way: God gives it, and the traveler's job is to take it. Third, an old memory. Aisha said, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the prayer was first prescribed as two units, then the traveler's prayer was kept that way while the prayer at home was lengthened. On that report, the shortened prayer is the older shape. Fourth, combining. On journeys the Prophet sometimes joined the noon and afternoon prayers, or sunset and night. Here the schools part ways. The Hanafi school holds shortening required for a traveler, and allows combining only during the hajj, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Other schools treat shortening as a permission and allow combining on journeys. They also differ on how far counts as a journey, and how long a stay ends it. Each reads the same reports with care.
screen: `FOUR BECOME TWO.` · `NO SIN TO CURTAIL.` · `A CHARITY: ACCEPT IT.` · `THE SCHOOLS PART WAYS.` · then, large: `ACCEPT HIS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Notice what you're carrying in your body, raised shoulders, a tight jaw, a gripping hand, and let one thing go with each breath; then bring your next trip to mind. If you pray, you might find out from a teacher or a trusted book of your school how far counts as a journey and whether you may combine. If you don't, notice one load you could set down on that trip.
Qasr. Shortening: on a journey, the four-unit prayers are prayed as two, a charity from God to accept. Today's word.
Your line: lighter on the road. A charity from God, there to be accepted. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims on a journey pray the noon, afternoon and night prayers as two units each, and depending on their school may combine noon with afternoon and sunset with night; schools set their own rules on distance and length of stay.

Every prayer drops to two units, dawn and sunset too, so it's the same for all.

chat.meaning: Four-unit prayers are prayed as two on a journey. Asked why, when people were safe, the Prophet said: it is a charity God has given you.

notes: Editor: new hook (a highway rest stop) because the airport-gate, delayed-flight scene repeated day 1073's hook; 'two days ago' corrected to 'four days ago' for duha (day 1083); dropped 'brave enough' as an unsupported characterization of the questioner. The 'Gate twelve' note no longer applies.
Pickthall 4:101 quoted from memory ('And when ye go forth in the land, it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship if ye fear that those who disbelieve may attack you'); confirm wording.

Muslim 686 (Ya'la ibn Umayyah, Umar, 'a charity ... accept His charity') paraphrased; Bukhari 350 (Aisha: prayer first enjoined as two rak'ahs) paraphrased; Bukhari 1107 cited for combining on journeys; confirm numbers.

Fiqh summary: Hanafi: qasr obligatory ('azimah) and jam' only at Arafah and Muzdalifah; Shafi'i, Hanbali, Maliki: qasr a concession or stressed sunnah, combining permitted for travel (with differences). Simplified; confirm. Distance and duration thresholds intentionally given without numbers.
'Gate twelve' is a scene detail, not a claim.
